name: SushiSwap RouteProcessor2 unvalidated route pool
summary: RouteProcessor2.processRoute() never checked that the pool address encoded in the caller-supplied `route` was a genuine UniswapV3 pool. The router called swap() on that address and then trusted whoever called back into uniswapV3SwapCallback(), whose implementation transfers `tokenIn` from the address recorded in the router's transient `lastCalledPool`/msg.sender state instead of from the caller. An attacker-controlled contract posing as a pool could therefore make the router execute transferFrom against any wallet that had granted RouteProcessor2 an ERC20 allowance.
notes: The non-upgradeable RouteProcessor2 runtime was installed by this direct CREATE and remained the exploit-executed code.

The depleted assets were not protocol-held funds. RouteProcessor2 custodies nothing; every wei taken came out of an external wallet that had previously granted the router an ERC20 allowance. Reconstructed from WETH Transfer receipts rather than from the post-mortem estimate: across eleven successful transactions between blocks 17007838 and 17007856, exactly eighteen 100 WETH transferFrom calls left the single approving wallet 0x31d3243cfb54b34fc9c73e1cb1137124bd6b13e1 for eight different searcher contracts, totalling exactly 1800.000000000000000000 WETH. Ten transactions moved 100 WETH each; 0x04b166e7b4ab5105a8e9c85f08f6346de1c66368687215b0e0b58d6e5002bc32 batched eight callbacks for 800 WETH. Sweeping every WETH inflow of all eight receiving contracts over blocks 16990000-17020000 turns up no other victim wallet, so the campaign's gross depletion is exactly the 1800 WETH the post-mortem approximates. Financing, gas, builder payments and any later whitehat returns are not netted.
The same defect was exploited against RouteProcessor2 deployments on other chains on the same day; those are separate deployments and separate campaigns.
